title: Games in a tree
objectives: Solve a sequential game by backward induction and spot threats nobody would carry out.

screens.title: Enter or stay out
screens.prose: A firm, the entrant, decides whether to enter a market. If it enters, the incumbent fights a price war or shares the market. Each end reads (Entrant's payoff, Incumbent's payoff), in £m.
screens.question: Tap the incumbent's move after entry, then the entrant's move.

hints.text: Start at the incumbent's node: what would it do once the entrant is in?
Fight pays the incumbent 2 and Share pays it 5.
Share, so In is worth 3 to the entrant, more than Out's 0.

feedback.correct: Share, then In: the game ends at (3, 5).
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide the incumbent's move first, then compare the entrant's two options.

byKey.threat: You let the incumbent fight. Once the entrant is in, fighting pays it 2 and sharing 5.
byKey.out-first: The incumbent shares, so entering pays the entrant 3. Staying out pays 0.

explain.text: After entry the incumbent compares 2 with 5 and shares. So In leads to (3, 5), and the entrant compares 3 with 0. It enters.

canvas.caption: Each node takes the payoff its mover picks: (3, 5) backs up to the root.

screens.title: The same game as a table
screens.prose: Write the game as a table. The entrant picks a row. The incumbent picks a plan, a column, saying what it does if the entrant comes in. Cells read (Entrant, Incumbent), in £m.
screens.question: Tap every pure Nash equilibrium of the table.

hints.text: Check each cell: can either player gain by changing alone?
In (Out, Fight), entering would pay the entrant −2, and the incumbent earns 10 either way.
Two cells: (Out, Fight) and (In, Share).

feedback.correct: (Out, Fight) and (In, Share) are both equilibria.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test every cell for a gain from moving alone.

byKey.tree-only: (In, Share) is one. In (Out, Fight), entering pays −2 against 0, and the incumbent's plan costs it nothing there.
byKey.out-only: (Out, Fight) is one, but (In, Share) is too: neither player gains by moving alone from it.

explain.text: Against Fight, Out (0) beats In (−2); against Out, the incumbent earns 10 with either plan. So (Out, Fight) is an equilibrium. (In, Share) is one too.

screens.title: Only one survives the tree
screens.prose: The table has two equilibria, but the tree gave only (In, Share).
screens.question: Why does (Out, Fight) fail in the tree?

options.text: Fight is a threat the incumbent would not carry out once the entrant is in
Out pays the entrant less than In against Fight
options.why: Against Fight, Out pays 0 and In −2, so Out is the better reply. The flaw is in the incumbent's plan.

options.text: The incumbent earns less at (Out, Fight)
options.why: It earns 10 there, its best payoff. The trouble is what it would do after entry.

options.text: A table cannot have two equilibria
options.why: Tables often have several, as lesson 3 showed. The tree rules one out.

hints.text: Ask what the incumbent does if the entrant does come in.
After entry, Fight pays it 2 and Share 5.
So the plan to fight would not be carried out.

feedback.correct: Fight is not credible: at its own node the incumbent shares.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the incumbent's choice after entry.

byKey.b: You checked the entrant's reply, which is fine. The plan to fight is what fails, at the incumbent's node.

explain.text: (Out, Fight) works only if the entrant believes the threat. At the node after entry, fighting pays 2 and sharing 5, so the threat is empty. An equilibrium that survives every node is **subgame perfect**.

screens.title: Take or pass
screens.prose: Ana and Ben take turns. At each node the mover may Take, ending the game, or Pass. Payoffs are (Ana, Ben) in £. Work from node 4 back to node 1.
screens.question: Fill in the payoff each node ends at, as Ana's, then Ben's.

hints.text: At node 4 Ben compares Take, 5 for him, with Pass, 4 for him.
Node 4 ends at (3, 5). At node 3 Ana compares Take's 4 with the 3 she gets from node 4.

feedback.correct: Each mover takes, so Ana takes at once: (2, 0).
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start at node 4 and compare the mover's own payoff for Take and for Pass.

byKey.r3c3: Node 1 is Ana's. Passing leads to node 2, where Ben takes (1, 3), so she takes 2.
byKey.r0c3: At node 4 Ben takes: 5 for him beats Pass's 4.
byKey.r1c3: At node 3 Ana takes 4, since passing leads to node 4's (3, 5) and only 3 for her.

explain.text: Ben takes at node 4 (5 > 4), so Ana takes at node 3 (4 > 3). Then Ben takes at node 2 (3 > 2), and Ana takes at once (2 > 1). Both would prefer (6, 4), but no mover trusts the next.

screens.title: A loud threat
screens.prose: Back to the entry game. Before anything happens, the incumbent announces that it will fight any entrant.
screens.question: What happens?

options.text: The entrant enters and the incumbent shares: (3, 5)

options.why: You took the threat at face value. After entry, fighting pays the incumbent 2 and sharing 5, so it shares.

options.text: The entrant enters and the incumbent fights: (−2, 2)
options.why: You assumed the incumbent keeps its word. Once the entrant is in, fighting costs it £3m.

hints.text: Words do not change the payoffs at the incumbent's node.
After entry: Fight 2, Share 5, for the incumbent.
So it shares, and the entrant enters.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve the incumbent's node as if no one had spoken.

byKey.b: You took the threat at face value. After entry, fighting pays the incumbent 2 and sharing 5, so it shares.

explain.text: A threat is credible only if its maker would carry it out when the time comes. After entry the incumbent earns 5 by sharing and 2 by fighting. The entrant knows it, ignores the threat and enters.

screens.title: A tie at the last node
screens.prose: Change one number: a price war now pays the incumbent 5, the same as sharing. Payoffs (Entrant, Incumbent) in £m.
screens.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: Both Out and In can be subgame perfect; it depends on how the incumbent breaks its tie
The entrant enters, since sharing still pays the incumbent 5
options.why: The incumbent could fight at no cost to itself. If it would, entering pays the entrant −2.

options.text: The entrant stays out, since the threat is now credible
options.why: Fighting is only as good as sharing for the incumbent, not better. Nothing forces it to fight.

hints.text: At the incumbent's node, both moves pay it 5.
If it fights, the entrant compares 0 with −2; if it shares, 0 with 3.
Two subgame perfect outcomes: (0, 10) and (3, 5).

feedback.correct: Right: a tie gives two subgame perfect equilibria.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the entrant's choice for each way the tie breaks.

byKey.c: You treated a tie as a promise. The incumbent is indifferent, so it might share.

explain.text: With a tie, fighting and sharing are both best replies after entry. If the incumbent fights, the entrant stays out, (0, 10); if it shares, the entrant enters, (3, 5). In an interview, say so and ask how ties break.

screens.title: Backward induction
screens.prose:
Start at the last decisions. Replace each by the payoff its mover picks, then work back to the root:

$$V(\text{node}) = \text{the child's } V \text{ with the mover's largest payoff}$$

This is `graphs-dp` l17-dice-stopping's $V = \max(\text{stop}, \text{go on})$, with two players. `brainteasers` l6-back-from-the-end uses it on longer chains.
screens.question: Where does backward induction start?

options.text: At the last decisions, then back towards the root
At the root, with the first mover's best end
options.why: The first mover's best end may need later movers to act against themselves, as (6, 4) did in the centipede.

options.text: At the end with the largest total payoff
options.why: Totals do not decide anything. Each mover keeps only their own payoff.

options.text: At the node where a threat is announced
options.why: Announcements change no payoff, so they change no node.

hints.text: Which choices can be made without knowing anything later?
The last movers face only end payoffs.
Start there and work back.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the choices that depend on nothing that comes after.

explain.text: The last movers choose between end payoffs, so their choices are fixed first. Each earlier mover then sees what follows each move. The result is the subgame perfect equilibrium: no threat in it is empty.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Four games, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the reasoning aloud before you answer. Two free resources hold more: the *Probability and Markets* guide and Open Yale Courses' *Game Theory* lectures. A trading firm wrote the guide about its own interviews. The tree shows the second game.
screens.question: Give Ana's payoff in each game.

rows: Six-move centipede. Take pays (2, 0), (1, 3), (4, 2), (3, 5), (6, 4), (5, 7). Pass at the end pays (8, 6).
The tree: Ana, then Ben, then Ana after Right and Pass
Lesson 4's venue game, Ana first. (X, X) pays (3, 2), (Y, Y) pays (2, 3), apart (0, 0).
The same venue game, Ben first

hints.text: Solve each from its last move back.
In the tree, after Right and Pass Ana takes (4, 1), so Ben ends at once with (2, 2).

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: (8, 6) needs everyone to pass. Ben takes at the last node, 7 against 6, and taking spreads back to node 1.
byKey.r1c1: Ana would take (4, 1) after Pass, so Ben, offered 1 there, ends at once with (2, 2).
byKey.r2c1: Ana moves first and picks X; Ben then matches, since 2 beats 0. Ana gets 3.
byKey.r3c1: Ben moves first and picks Y; Ana matches, since 2 beats 0. Ana gets 2.

explain.text: Six moves: Ben takes at the last node (7 > 6) and taking runs back, so Ana takes at once, 2. The tree: Ben ends after Right (2 > 1) and plays Down after Left, so Ana picks Right, 2. In the venue game the first mover picks a favourite and the other follows: 3, then 2.

screens.title: Follow-up: buying capacity
screens.prose: The interviewer lets the incumbent buy spare capacity first, at a cost of $k$, in £m. With it a price war is cheap: after entry, Fight pays the incumbent 6 − k and Share 5 − k. The entrant's payoffs do not change.
screens.question: What is the most the incumbent should pay for the capacity, in £m?

widget.accept: 5: with capacity it keeps 10 − k, against 5 without it.

hints.text: With capacity, compare Fight and Share after entry.
6 − k beats 5 − k, so fighting is now credible and the entrant stays out.
Capacity pays 10 − k; without it the incumbent gets 5. So k up to 5.

feedback.correct: £5m: it keeps 10 − k with the capacity and 5 without.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what the incumbent ends with, with and without the capacity.

byKey.ten: Staying out leaves it 10 − k, not 10. Without capacity it gets 5, so it pays up to 10 − 5.
byKey.one: £1m is what fighting gains over sharing. The real prize is keeping the market: 10 − k against 5.

explain.text: With capacity, Fight beats Share by £1m, so the threat is credible and the entrant stays out. It keeps 10 − k, against 5 without, so it pays up to £5m. A desk that publishes a hard risk limit buys the same credibility.

ideas: Solve a tree from its last decisions back to the root, each mover keeping their best child.
A threat its maker would not carry out at its own node is not credible, and the tree discards it.
Paying to change your own later payoffs, such as spare capacity, can make a threat credible.

formula.name: Backward induction
formula.tex: V(\text{node}) = V(\text{child that maximises the mover's payoff})
formula.note: Start at the leaves; the root's value is the subgame perfect outcome.

summary.trap: Believing an announced threat. Check what the threat's maker would do when the time comes.

quiz.prose: A new entry game. Payoffs (Entrant, Incumbent) in £m: Out (0, 7); after entry, Fight (−3, 3) or Share (1, 2).
quiz.question: What does the entrant do?

options.why: You assumed the incumbent shares. Here fighting pays it 3 and sharing 2, so the threat is real.

feedback.correct: Stays out: the incumbent would fight, 3 against 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve the incumbent's node first.

explain.text: After entry the incumbent earns 3 by fighting and 2 by sharing, so it fights. Entering then pays the entrant −3, against 0 for staying out. Here the threat is credible.

quiz.prose: Ana moves first. Safe ends the game at (2, 2). Risky hands Ben a choice between (5, 1) and (0, 3). Payoffs (Ana, Ben) in £.
quiz.question: What is Ana's payoff?

widget.accept: 2: Ben would pick (0, 3) after Risky, so Ana plays Safe.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide Ben's move after Risky first.

byKey.five: (5, 1) needs Ben to accept 1 when 3 is on offer. He picks (0, 3).
byKey.zero: That is what Risky brings. Ana sees it coming and plays Safe for 2.

explain.text: After Risky, Ben picks (0, 3), since 3 beats 1. So Risky is worth 0 to Ana and Safe 2. She plays Safe.

quiz.prose: Chicken in turn. Each driver swerves or goes straight. (Swerve, Swerve) pays (2, 2), (Swerve, Straight) (1, 3), (Straight, Swerve) (3, 1), (Straight, Straight) (0, 0). Ana moves first; Ben sees her move.
quiz.question: What is Ana's payoff?

widget.accept: 3: she goes straight and Ben swerves.

feedback.correct: £3: Ana commits to Straight and Ben swerves.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out Ben's reply to each of Ana's moves.

byKey.two: (2, 2) needs Ben to swerve after Ana swerves, but then Straight pays him 3.
byKey.one: That is Ana swerving first. Going straight instead makes Ben swerve, 1 against 0.

explain.text: If Ana goes straight, Ben swerves (1 > 0), giving Ana 3. If she swerves, Ben goes straight (3 > 2), giving her 1. Moving first lets Ana commit, so she takes 3.
